description:
Farideh ÄŒabarkapa-Sow is slight and fidgety, with the kind of face that people struggle to describe afterward â€” deliberately so. They have medium-brown skin and keep their hair a different color every two weeks, courtesy of color-changing follicle geneware, currently a deep teal that fades to bronze at the tips. They have a faint bioluminescent pulse along their collarbones that they usually cover with high-necked clothing, a mod from a phase a few years ago that they haven't had removed because it costs more to undo than to keep. Their fingers are rarely still â€” they're always rolling something between them, a stylus, a coin, a small tool â€” and they tend to look at surfaces rather than people when they talk, as though they're reading information off of whatever they're looking at.

Farideh ÄŒabarkapa-Sow is brilliant at the specific thing they do, which is making people into other people on paper â€” or, more precisely, in the vast interlocking authentication lattices that determine who gets to be who in GLMZ. They design identities the way some people design architecture: with attention to load-bearing details, to how structures weather over time, to what fails first under pressure. They work alone, price fairly by Shallowgrave standards, and have a waiting list. They do not take jobs that feel like someone is going to die because of the identity. They are not always right about when that is.

being so thoroughly identified by the system that no counter-identity will protect them
core_desires: to be recognized as an artist, not just a criminal service provider

psychology.secret: Their own legal identity is built on a fabrication â€” they have no recoverable original documentation. They were born in circumstances they've never fully investigated, to parents who may have been running from something. They have constructed four layers of identity around the gap, but the gap is still there, and sometimes they find themselves trying to forge backward into their own past.

example_lines: 'Okay so the thing most people don't get is that an identity isn't a document, it's a load-bearing story, and if you don't know where the weight sits you'll build something that looks fine and then collapses the first time someone leans on it.'

'I don't do deaths. I don't mean I won't forge a death certificate â€” I mean I don't take commissions that structurally require someone on the other end to end up dead. That's my one rule. I've been wrong about it twice.'
